title: Long-term audit archive policy and RT indexing strategy for admin events
creator: Asha Patel
description: Design and implement a two-tier audit storage strategy plus a real-time (RT) indexing approach for high-value admin/security events (RBAC v2 changes, SSO/SAML admin flows, key rotations, consent/grants). Goals: keep recent admin events queryable with low latency, ensure tamper-evident long-term archive with predictable cost, support per-customer retention SLAs, and provide lifecycle controls (auto-archive, purge, sampling for low-sensitivity events). This ticket covers ingestion pipeline changes, indexing strategy, partitioning scheme, storage lifecycle policies, cost-control knobs, and migration plan for existing audit data.
acceptance_criteria: Admin and security-critical events (actor, action, target, timestamp, request_id) are ingested with idempotency and appear in the RT index within 10s for >= 99% of events.
Queries for admin events over the last 30 days have median latency < 300ms for typical filters (org_id + action_type + time range).
Hot storage retention defaults and per-org overrides are configurable: default hot=90d, warm=2y, cold=7y (policy driven).
Archive layer stores full raw events in columnar, compressed format (Parquet) in S3 with an immutable manifest for auditability.
A lifecycle job moves data across tiers automatically and emits metrics (bytes moved, cost projection) to dashboards.
Storage cost controls (sampling thresholds, size-based compaction, TTL enforcement) are implemented and covered by tests and a cost-simulation run for a 1PB/year ingest profile.
Security review completed and SRE runbook added for archive recoveries and corruption detection.
Migration path and backfill plan for existing 18 months of audit logs documented and staged (no downtime required for live queries).
tasks: Audit ingestion: add event_id idempotency, Avro schema v3, and mandatory org_id and actor_id fields
Streaming enrichment: use Flink job to attach RBAC v2 deltas (pre/post perms) and SAML metadata to events
RT index: deploy sharded OpenSearch index optimized by time+org hash with ILM (index lifecycle management) policies
Partitioning: primary partition by YYYY-MM + org_hash prefix; secondary index fields: action_type, actor_id
Archive writer: palletized Parquet writer to s3://redwood-audit-archive/{year}/{month}/{org}/ with manifest checksums
Lifecycle controller: Lambda/cron job to transition indices -> parquet -> glacier and emit metrics
Cost controls: implement sampling rules for low-sensitivity telemetry events and size-based compaction for high-cardinality orgs
Backfill plan: write idempotent backfill job and dry-run on a 30-day window, validate query parity
Dashboarding: add panels for ingest lag, archive throughput, monthly storage cost projection
Run security review and tabletop recovery drill
design_decisions: Two-tier model: Hot RT index (OpenSearch) for 90d by default; Warm/Cold in S3 as Parquet with an immutable manifest. Chosen for query latency vs cost tradeoff.
Partitioning uses a composite key: time_bucket (YYYY-MM) + org_hash(6) to keep hot shards bounded for large tenants.
Index fields are limited to small, frequently-filtered attributes; large blobs (full request/response) are stored only in raw archive to reduce index size.
Idempotency: rely on provided event_id; ingestion will dedupe based on event_id at Kafka consumer level to avoid duplicates from retries.
Privacy: PII fields are redacted at ingestion for non-admin teams; full raw payload retained encrypted in cold archive where required by compliance.
Sampling: non-security telemetry events (info-level) default to 10% sampling for older-than-90d data unless org opts-in for full retention.
Tamper-evidence: manifest + checksum + signed commit records for each archive batch to support audits and legal hold requests.
tradeoffs: Keeping larger datasets in OpenSearch improves analytic latency but increases cost—we mitigate with strict ILM and per-org caps.
Storing full payloads only in archive increases restore complexity if ad-hoc deep-dive is required, but reduces hot-store costs and index bloat.
Using Parquet on S3 for cold storage delays ad-hoc queries (need query engine like Athena) versus keeping everything in OpenSearch; chosen due to cost at scale.
Adding enrichment (RBAC deltas) in the stream increases ingestion cost and complexity but makes post-hoc queries far more actionable for security teams.
implementation_notes: Kafka topic: audit.events.v3, use 6 partitions initially, increase based on org load
Schema registry: bump to v3 (see registry URL in links), consumers must fail-fast on incompatible schema
Flink job: enrichment must be idempotent and checkpointed; use exactly-once semantics where available
OpenSearch mapping: disable _all, set doc_values on filter fields, use keyword for actor_id and action_type
S3 writes: use multipart upload with atomic manifest commit to avoid partial batch visibility
Run cost-sim: ingest synthetic 1PB/year dataset into staging using current mappings and measure projected monthly S3+OpenSearch costs
